utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Good morning, everyone. Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, good morning, Mr. President. I'd like to introduce David Taylor of Manchester, United Kingdom, who is working as an intern for us this year.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Mitchell, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I understand I have about an hour left. I'll do my best to conclude in that time, but I may need a little extra. I'll let you know where I'm at when the hour is up.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Kos, yesterday we left off and I was asking you some questions about your interview with the Slovenian investigator.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we can have that in e-court again, 65 ter 25487, page 2 in the English and 3 in the Slovenian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, if you just focus on that paragraph at the top in your language where it says: "According to his estimation, approximately 1.000 Muslims were killed ..." Now, yesterday I asked you whether this was accurate, what you had told the Slovenian investigator. And you said, this is a quote from page 110 of yesterday's transcript, line 1, you said: "Yes, but I referred to Erdemovic's statement there." Now, you can see in that sentence where it says: "According to his estimation, approximately 1.000 Muslims were killed ..." There's no reference to Drazen Erdemovic there. That's your estimation, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That estimation - let me explain - always referred to Drazen Erdemovic's statement and that's what we all thought based on his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So you agreed with Drazen Erdemovic's estimate that approximately 1.000 Muslims were killed at Branjevo Farm on 16 July?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We have to make a distinction here. At Branjevo Farm, people were killed. Two things are being confused here: How many were killed and how many were buried. If a thousand had been killed at Branjevo and we are charged with an extra 500, where were these people buried then? There is a distinction being made here between those who were killed at Branjevo Farm and those who were subsequently buried at Branjevo Farm. It is a well-known fact from my trial that people kept on being brought in lorries to Branjevo Farm. I even said in my interview with Tomasz Blaszczyk that people must have been executed elsewhere because those people who arrived after the buses, once we stopped killing, looked as if they had been executed elsewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Kos, the evidence in our case - this is Exhibit P4772, Dusan Janc's report - is that there's 1.735 individuals have been identified by DNA matching out of the Branjevo Farm grave and its associated secondary graves. It's our case that approximately 500 of those 1700 were killed at the Pilica Dom, which leaves approximately 1200 individuals who were executed at Branjevo Farm; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me explain in this way. We're running in circles here. You're insisting on one figure and I am persistently saying that I based my statement on Drazen Erdemovic's statement. I always adhere by my words. At Branjevo Farm the 10th Sabotage Unit did not execute more than six buses, a total of seven to seven and a half of people -- buses arrived, and this is what I've always claimed and I always will. At my trial the witnesses stated, and it was proven by the size of the grave that was found at Branjevo, and nobody ever wanted to prove what its dimensions were, and you have its dimensions in my first-instance judgement. That's where they are given, the exact dimensions are given there. In our order to make up for 1200 or to 1800 Muslims, which were the two figures mention during my trial, in one part of the first-instance judgement, the Trial Chamber wrote that there were several graveyards or graves found at Branjevo Farm. In a paragraph before that it says that there was just one grave at Branjevo Farm and its exact dimensions are mentioned. The only thing that is not mentioned is the name of the person who opened it, William Haglund. His name was deliberately omitted during my trial so that he did not have to be brought as a witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Well, yesterday you agreed that it wasn't in your interest to inflate or exaggerate in any way the number of Muslims who were killed at Branjevo Farm. So regardless of whether this figure that you told the Slovenian investigator is your estimation or Drazen Erdemovic's estimation, there's absolutely no reason whatsoever for you to have mentioned a figure of 1.000 if you actually thought that some 350 to 370 people were killed at Branjevo Farm that day; right? That doesn't make any sense whatsoever, does it?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I keep on telling you, that was in 2004. As far as I can remember, the Slovenian investigator took the interview in Bijeljina -- or actually, that's where he wrote his wrote, in a restaurant in Bijeljina from memory, from what I had stated. I provided the statement and he memorised it. As far as I can remember, my words were not recorded. He did not record my words, and I keep on claiming that I said in 2004, when the trial started, that so many people had been killed. That's what I thought at the time. I hadn't given it a second thought. But now I claim with full responsibility, I don't intend to insult the victims, that the 10th Sabotage Unit did not execute more than six buses and the overall number of people who were executed at Branjevo Farm was not more than eight busloads. It doesn't make any difference to me. Even if I reduce the figure, the things are the same for me. Even if we killed one innocent civilian, which is terrible, or 300 because we had been ordered to execute those prisoners of war, it still would have been a big crime. But we couldn't do anything there and we have been held responsible even more than some local individuals who were behind that. We didn't have a clue what we would be doing at Branjevo when we first arrived there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, let me just remind you of something you said yesterday. This is at transcript page 103 of yesterday's provisional transcript. You said: "I can't tell you how many buses there were. I was not in the Kula school, I was not in Pilica -- actually, it's one and the same. How many buses there were and what make they were, I really can't remember as I sit here today, nor can I answer your question." Do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't tell you how many buses there were in front of the Kula school. I was never in front of the Kula school. To this very day, I've never been there. I don't know where that school is. Whatever you told me yesterday, those are the statements provided by a survivor who was there. I believe that that's what you said. During my trial a statement was provided before the BH court by the bus driver who had brought those prisoners of war from Bratunac to the Kula school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, we'll get to -- we'll get to what was said in your trial about this. Let me go first to your interview with Mr. Blaszczyk on the 8th of May, 2010, this is 65 ter 25482, page 143 in English and 96 in the B/C/S. And again, we can agree that it's not in your interest to exaggerate the number of Muslims who were killed at the farm, is it, to give a higher number than actually were killed by your unit?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't benefit from that at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Well, Mr. Blaszczyk asked you: "... how many people were killed that day? Your estimation?" Not Drazen Erdemovic's estimation. Your estimation. And you said: "On Branjevo the assessment is 650-700 ..." So that is twice the number that you told Mr. Karadzic's Defence lawyer earlier this year, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Hold on, hold on. I apologise. You'll have to repeat that question, I'm afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can you see in line 4 in your language --

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I see that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- your words: "On Branjevo the assessment is 650-700 people." All I'm asking is that number that you gave in 2010 is twice the number that you told Mr. Karadzic's Defence lawyer earlier this year, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it says 650-700 people here. I repeat once again, I'm referring to Drazen Erdemovic's statement here. I did not exaggerate the number of those who were killed; however, I also referred to the statements given by some people who said later on that that's how many had been killed. One of the witnesses --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Let me stop you --

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- said --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Let me stop you there. Mr. Blaszczyk's question was your estimation. He asked you for your estimation and you said: " ... the assessment is 650-700 people." There's no mention of Drazen Erdemovic, no mention of anyone else, this is your estimation in 2010; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's my estimation. This is what it says here, this is what I stated. But I repeat, based on your people's statements as well as the facts that were established here before this Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can we have 65 ter number 25481 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: This is your interview with the state court prosecutor in August 2010. And you'll remember at the start of that interview the prosecutor said to you had the right to put forward your own defence, you had the right to remain silent, and you were also told that anything you said could be used in evidence in your trial against you. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Are you referring to Tomasz Blaszczyk or to the prosecutor before the BiH court?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: We're now talking about the BiH prosecutor interview. This is a different one now.

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. So you remember the prosecutor telling you you could put forward your defence, you could stay silent, but that if you did say anything that could be used as evidence against you. You remember that?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Can we go to page 33 in both languages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And you will see here -- so, in this interview where you were putting forward your own Defence you say: "... I don't think more than about 600 people ..." So again, not Drazen Erdemovic, not anyone else, this is your estimate in this interview, 600; right? Can you see in line 6 your words?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, these are my words.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Now let's go to the testimony in your own case in 2011. And you remember at the start of your testimony the judge warned you that it was your duty to tell the truth because perjury is crime; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. And in your own trial, of all places, where your own freedom is at stake, it's in your very best interest not to exaggerate the number of people who were killed at Branjevo Farm, is it?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Well, in your testimony, unfortunately we don't have a transcript of it in your language, but it's 65 ter 25480, page 95 in the English, you give two estimates. First of all you say 300 and then under cross-examination at page 137 you say "probably 600." And then in the judgement in your case, which I'll bring up and let you have a look at, 65 ter 25492, page 103 in the B/C/S, if you look at paragraph 575 it says: [As read] "The accused - Franc Kos - also participated in the executions. Over the course of his testimony, Kos kept changing the number of buses and prisoners killed, stating at the end ... that a total of almost 8 buses of prisoners were killed at Branjevo, the last of which having been half full ..." So even in your own case where your own freedom was at stake, you're testifying under penalty perjury, even then you couldn't keep your story straight, could you, about how many buses and how many people were killed that day?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: When I testified on my own behalf, as I already told you yesterday, explained how the executions were carried out. I know what happened with each of the buses. That's why I came up with the number of eight buses in total.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. But as you're sitting here today, 18 years later, we've seen you've gone from telling the Slovenian investigator ten years ago an estimate of 1.000; then you told Mr. Blaszczyk 650 to 700; then you told the state court prosecutor 600; then in your own trial you went between 300 and 600. As you sit here today, you can't say with any certainty how many prisoners were killed at Branjevo Farm that day, can you?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm telling you again and again how many were killed, but I don't know how many dead bodies were dragged into the place subsequently. I keep on telling you how many were executed while we were there at Branjevo Farm, how many were killed by the 10th Sabotage Unit and that other group.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you again. 2004, you've gone from giving the investigator an estimate of a thousand, now you're down to 300; and in between you've given a range of estimates, 650 to 700, 600. As you sit here today, you can't say with any certainty whether it's 300, 600, 650, 700, or a thousand, can you? With a hundred per cent certainty, you can't say what the number is, can you?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that nobody can say that with any certainty. Nobody can say how many were executed at Branjevo Farm, how many exactly were killed and how many were buried there. There's just one man who can say how many were buried.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Let's move to something completely different. May or June 1995 you and the other members of your unit went through a mine tunnel near Srebrenica and you conducted an operation against the town, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which town?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Against the town of Srebrenica. You went through the mine tunnel and then you fired some weapons into the town of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you haven't been to Srebrenica before and you weren't familiar with the layout of the town and it was the middle of the night; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was the first operation for which we were brought. In the evening we went through the tunnel and we came back. That was the first time. Until then, I had never been in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. Then, when we entered, I did not know the exact purpose of this operation. It was only when we got out that we found out what the purpose of that operation was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. And after you'd come out of the mine tunnel, your unit fired a 60-millimetre mortar, some Zoljas, and some Osa missiles into the town; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what they were being fired at because I don't know the exact location where we were. I know that we were on a hill above Srebrenica. Below there were white roofs that we could see at night. Now, whether these were some factories were something, I cannot say, so I cannot say what we fired these projectiles at.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. But the aim was basically to just fire as many projectiles as possible as quickly as you could and get out of there; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I have to say something there. All these projectiles that we fired were Zoljas, Osas. None of that reached an inhabited area. All these projectiles, when fired at a certain range, self-destruct. So a Zolja, M60, self-destructs at a range of 450 to 500 metres I think. And an Osa at 650 to 700 metres, it self destructs unless it hits a target. My estimate is that we must have been at a distance of at least 1.500 metres from that inhabited area when we were up on the hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. You told Mr. Blaszczyk in your interview with him that it was your view that the purpose of this mission was to create chaos in Srebrenica; is that right? By firing these weapons towards Srebrenica, the purpose was to create chaos?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is what we were told when we got out. The operation had been carried out to show sort of that there is chaos in Srebrenica and that soldiers, Muslims, started fighting amongst themselves, quarrelling amongst themselves, and to create some kind of chaos amongst the population and a lack of safety and security. That's what we were told when we got out, when the operation was over.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Let's go now to the 11th of July, so the day when your unit entered the town of Srebrenica. Now, as you were approaching the town that day and as you were entering the town, you were talking to the other members of your unit on the Motorola -- on the Motorola radios, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we had radio communication with the other groups.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. And at one point you heard General Krstic over the radio, the commander of the Srebrenica operation, and you heard him say the words: "Push and burn down"; correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't see the point of this push and burn down. What --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I'm not asking you to -- the point. I'm saying you heard General Krstic say that over the radio, over the Motorola; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Because when we started entering Srebrenica, first of all, in the morning we had not left immediately so we had to get down into Srebrenica in haste. As for this thing, push and burn down, that means that one should advance and that in -- along the way something should be torched, a haystack or whatever, but in that way people would know how far our unit had advanced, our people would know for the sake of security how far we had advanced down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, let me remind you of what you told Mr. Blaszczyk in your interview in 2010.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we can have 65 ter 25482 in e-court, that's English page 41, B/C/S page 28.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And you'll see when this comes up you said: "We heard him," that's General Krstic, "saying, 'Push and burn down,' but we did not want to set fire to houses because we understood that he meant that houses should be put on fire." So that's what you understood General Krstic to be saying, isn't it? He was ordering you to set houses on fire as you came into Srebrenica. Can you see the paragraph in the middle of the page? You say: " ... we understood that he meant houses should be put on fire," and then you go on to explain that you didn't want to set houses on fire. So let me ask you again: When General Krstic said "Push and burn down," you understood that to be an order to set fire to houses, right?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, we thought that that's the way it was; however, we did not torch houses. We torched hay. That was our opinion. He did not issue that kind of order. I expressed my own opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. So it's your opinion that General Krstic was telling you to burn houses, but your unit didn't actually burn any houses. Do I understand you correctly?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was my opinion. As far as I can remember, not a single house was torched as we were going down there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you stayed in Srebrenica on the night of the 11th and then all day on the 12th. And Lieutenant Pelemis authorised your unit to go into some of the houses and take some of the items, like kitchen appliances, that kind of thing, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. And you ended up taking a truck and a trailer full of items out of Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, on 11 and 12th July, most of the Muslim population was just up the road in Potocari, weren't they, up near the UN base?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that because I did not go to Potocari. I went to the centre of Srebrenica on the 11th and I went back and I never came back there. I can confirm that. As far as Potocari is concerned, I don't know anything about that. As for what you said, civilians, there were civilians in Srebrenica when we entered, but we provided security for them. As for Potocari, I cannot say anything about that because I wasn't there and I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, you didn't provide security for all of them, did you? Zoran Obrenovic slit the throat of one of them, didn't he, when he surrendered to your unit?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That man, when I got down there into town, he was already dead. As for Zoran Obrenovic slitting his throat, I heard about that from other people. I did not see that with my own eyes, that he had slit his throat.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Right. But you saw his dead body lying on the sidewalk in town, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw his body.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Well, on the 11th and 12th of July when General Krstic is ordering that some things be burned and your unit is removing things from the Muslim houses, it must have been very obvious to you then that those Muslims weren't coming back to Srebrenica; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was a nobody over there. I was not supposed to think about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I understand that, but you wouldn't -- your unit wouldn't have been taking things from the homes of those Muslim people if they were coming back, would you?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How do we know that these were only Muslim houses?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It's for the witness to answer. Witness could be able to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Let me ask my question again, Mr. Kos. Your unit wouldn't have been taking things from Muslim homes in Srebrenica if those Muslim people were coming back to their homes, would you?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: These were houses. They were not apartments. Whose houses they were, I don't know. Now, whether people were supposed to come back, that I don't know. Who planned to do what further on with these people, I don't know, and I don't see the point of these questions. To me as a soldier who just came there, carried out an order, and everything I say here about this is just my opinion. I can just express my own opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. One last question on this. Lieutenant Pelemis gave you the green light, he gave you permission to go in and take things from those apartments or from those houses, didn't he? I'm not accusing you of anything. I'm just saying Lieutenant Pelemis said you could go and do that?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't say that to me personally. Who he said that to, I don't know. I just help people with the loading, and now whether he said that to someone you will have to ask Milorad Pelemis personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to Kravica on 13 July. Now, in your statement or your interview with Mr. Karadzic's lawyer, you said that around 6.00 p.m. on the 13th of July you, Marko Boskic, and Lieutenant Pelemis went to the command post in Vlasenica; correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Whose command post?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: The Drina Corps command post in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the Drina Corps in Vlasenica. I'm asking because our command was in Vlasenica as well, in a village by Vlasenica, that's why I'm asking whose command, because we went from our command in Dragosevci in the corps to the command in Vlasenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you. I'll be more precise. Now, Lieutenant Pelemis went inside the Drina Corps command post and he spoke with General Krstic, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he entered the command of the Drina Corps. Now, who he talked to, I have no way of knowing. Officers were inside. Now, which officers he talked to I cannot say because they talked behind closed doors. I and Boskic stood in front, in a big hall.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go back to 65 ter 25482. This is your ICTY interview again. It's page 50 in the English, page 34 in the B/C/S. And you say here: "Pelemis talked to some people I didn't know. Later I've seen those people on some other locations -- in some other locations where I have seen General Krstic. I learned then that it was General Krstic." So you might not have known right at the time, but later on you learned it was General Krstic who was talking to Pelemis at the Drina Corps command; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I explained that to you a moment ago. Who he talked to and what he talked about, I have no way of knowing. He can talk to any man who is at the command at the time and also to the general because they know each other personally, and some colonel and some officer who's a neighbour of his -- now, what they talk about, I don't know. They were present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. So General Krstic was present there. You learned later that the officer that Pelemis was talking to was General Krstic? I'm not asking you what they were talking about. I'm just saying that General Krstic was there; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. So you leave the Drina Corps command and you start heading towards Kravica. So you're driving towards Konjevic Polje. And Lieutenant Pelemis says to you and Marko Boskic, this is what you said in the state court in your own testimony: "We have to go to Kravica. There has been an incident there. We have some people there. There are dead prisoners also." So that was your testimony in the state court. Do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But I don't remember that I said "to Kravica." He said: Let's go and take a ride to Konjevic Polje and further on. I'm not 100 per cent sure that he mentioned Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. But he did say: "There's been an incident ... we have some people there. There are dead prisoners also." That's what you said in your testimony in the state court. Do you stand by that?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. So you drove to Konjevic Polje and then you turned right and you went down the road to Kravica and you went past the warehouse and parked your car about a hundred metres past the warehouse on the right-hand side of the road. And Pelemis got out and he went and spoke with five senior officers who were standing there with their jeeps. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. And you actually saw these five officers in some other actions and you thought that -- you didn't know exactly who they were, but you thought that they were from the VRS Main Staff in Han Pijesak; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I thought then.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because people were in jeeps, that is to say military jeeps. Who was in the military jeep, I don't know, because they had such jeeps in corps commands and in brigade commands, brigade commanders. That is just my opinion. I cannot say that with 100 per cent certainty and I cannot claim that these are people from the Main Staff either.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. But you knew that they were officers from the VRS, right, because of their uniforms, their appearance, their attitude, you knew that these were officers; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And you overheard one of these officers say something to Pelemis like, this is a quote from your ICTY interview, 65 ter 25482, the officer said to Pelemis: "They made a big mess. We have to bury all this and hide it." So you heard one of those officers say that to Lieutenant Pelemis?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. So you've marked about a hundred metres away. You then walk up to the warehouse, and on the way you heard two explosions, two grenade explosions, and four or five shots as you're walking towards the warehouse; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that was near the warehouse. Now, whether it was in the warehouse, I don't know because I did not see and there was still fighting going on there, there was still shooting because nearby these Muslim soldiers were passing by above that hangar. I heard two explosions and bursts of gun-fire. Now, whether that was in the warehouse or behind the warehouse, I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, when you arrive at the warehouse, you saw that the warehouse had basically two main rooms, right, a big one on the left and a big one on the right?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. And you looked in the room on the left side of the warehouse, so the end that's closest to Bratunac, and you saw that the entire floor of that side of the warehouse was covered in dead bodies; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I saw bodies from the bus to the entrance into the warehouse. I did not see bodies in the warehouse then, when I got to the warehouse. I saw them in front of the warehouse, bodies, not to go into estimates again. Perhaps it would be about 20 human bodies.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Can I have 65 ter 25483 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: This is a sketch of the Kravica warehouse that you drew during your interview with Mr. Blaszczyk in 2010. Now, that's your signature on the left, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. And we can see on the room on the left -- so you've drawn the warehouse. On the room on the left you've written a number 8; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And on the room on the right you've written a number 9?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. If we go now to 65 ter 25482, your interview, and we'll see what you had to say what you saw in those two rooms marked number 8 and number 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So if we can go to page 61 in the English and 42 in the B/C/S.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And we can see here the area you marked with an 8 is the area where you saw the dead bodies. And you say: "Yes. "The entire area? "Yes." So you did look in the left-hand side that was marked with a number 8 and the entire area was covered with bodies; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. This has to do with the dead bodies outside, because when the man said there are some inside then I approached the warehouse and a wounded prisoner ran out of the warehouse. I spoke about that there. Then I saw that there were bodies there, not before that. Only when I got to the door. Before that, I didn't know that there were dead people inside as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: But, Mr. Kos, that was your sketch. You put a number 8 on the area where you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we go back and starting -- start from where he explained the numbers and the location. I think it -- the English page should go back by one page. Why don't you start from number 7.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: We can start from number 7, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Do you see it in B/C/S as well?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So perhaps we can go back to the image, 65 ter 25483 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Why don't we print it out and give the witness a hard copy print-out. Also, we would like to have a -- I think the Registrar could do that. 65 ter number 25483, and distribute it to the witness and the Chamber. And --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Perhaps I can deal with something else --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- briefly and come back to this, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: When you were leaving Kravica and you were heading back towards your base at Dragasevac, you said to Pelemis, Lieutenant Pelemis: "Boss, if it's possible, do not get us involved in this because it is not a human thing to do. This is not a job for us." Do you remember saying something like that to Lieutenant Pelemis after you left Kravica and you were heading back to your base?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that to Pelemis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And Pelemis said to you: "From this point on, whoever calls you by phone or summons you asking you to go there, you shouldn't go anywhere until I get there. Just tell them: I have my superior officer, he will give the orders." So that's what -- you know, when you said to Pelemis: Don't let us get involved in this, Pelemis said: Don't do anything unless I approve it. Right?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't say: Don't do anything unless I approve it. He said that I mustn't budge from the base without his approval.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the job, the execution, we didn't talk about that. This was after Kravica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: And it was clear that people were avenging themselves, having their own personal vengeances. I saw that with my own eyes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Right. And you were asking Pelemis for your unit not to be involved, and he said: Don't do anything unless I approve it. So don't go anywhere without my permission; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not the execution that was meant by that. He wasn't to take the unit to such places as Kravica. That's what I meant then. I didn't have the execution in mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you just said it was clear that people were avenging themselves, having their own personal vengeances. The special police brigade who was at Kravica participating in those executions there weren't carrying out personal vengeances, were they?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which special police brigade you mean. Which brigade? Which platoon? Which company? Because I didn't see anyone from a special police brigade there. There was some six to seven soldiers wearing camouflage uniforms, older uniforms. And as far as I was able to notice during my stay at Kravica by that warehouse, two or three executions for personal reasons were carried out, and the reason was some personal -- were some personal axes that they had to grind from before the war --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- okay so --

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- they had an argument before the war and --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: There are two or three personal revenge killings at Kravica. The rest are an organised execution; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that. I know that there was an incident when one of the prisoners grabbed a rifle and started shooting at the guards, and I heard that one was killed and two wounded. And then shooting started in front of the hangar. I don't know who killed the people inside the hangar. I have no way of knowing --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- I wasn't present.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. And your unit that went to Branjevo Farm on the 16th of July didn't go there because of personal vengeance, did it? You went there because you were ordered to go there; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: We never received orders to go to the Branjevo Farm. Our order was that we were supposed to secure prisoners. No one ever mentioned Branjevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. The point was, though, you didn't kill prisoners at the Branjevo Farm because of personal vengeance, did you? You did it because you were ordered to do it?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one member of the 10th Sabotage Detachment - and I'm speaking about the 1st Platoon - had any personal reasons or ethnically based reasons to go there. The 10th Sabotage Detachment did what it did because they were ordered to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go back to the picture of Kravica --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Mitchell, I leave it to you whether to lead this or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But did we hear what he did in Kravica warehouse?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I'm just getting to that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So if you look at the picture that's here, look at the big room where you put an 8. And you can see just to the right of that there's a pole that you've marked with a 7; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. And just outside that room we can see a number 5, and the number 5 is where you were standing when you looked into the room that's marked with a number 8?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I approached the place and watched the dead bodies --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry to interrupt, but could we have this --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Zecevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZECEVIC
utterances.text: -- photo on the -- on the e-court, please? The drawing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. We could put it on the ELMO as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: We can, Mr. President, but I do want to stay -- [overlapping speakers] --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, yes, we will stay. But was this print-out provided to Mr. Zecevic as well? Yes. But shall we continue, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: So you're standing at the point marked with a number 5, you're looking into the room that you marked with a number 8, and you said to Mr. Blaszczyk the entire floor of this room that you've marked with an 8 was covered in bodies. And again, I'm not accusing you of anything, I'm just asking you: You looked in there and you saw this room, the floor of this room covered with bodies? That's what you told Mr. Blaszczyk in your interview in 2010.

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that the floor was covered with bodies, but I thought that they were sleeping. That's why I approached the door --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- and I experienced what I did at the door.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. And you also looked into the room on the right-hand side that's marked with a number 9.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If we can go to the next page in the English in the interview.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And you saw that the room on the right-hand side, so this is the room closest to Konjevic Polje, it was also full of dead people; correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The room was full, but one could still hear a murmuring inside, people speaking. That's why I thought that in the right warehouse they were still alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. And the right room, the one marked with a number 9, that's the one that -- where you heard people murmuring, that's the one that Marko Boskic went and threw two grenades into, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: He didn't enter the room --

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: He stood outside the room and threw the grenades inside?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When I returned to the room, he approached the warehouse and threw two grenades inside. And most probably he had spoken to one of the guards there about what had been happening during the day so that he too ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, can I tender that sketch?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: No objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What does "slika" mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Kos, perhaps you could explain. On the top left of your sketch what does "slika" mean written on the top left?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: "Portrait," "drawing." "Sketch," if you will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, we'll admit this.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Exhibit P6473, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Let's go back very briefly to your interview -- or the notes of your interview with the Slovenian investigator in 2004, 65 ter 25487, and that's page 3 in both languages in the English and the Slovenian. And in the third paragraph down in your language you'll see it says: "From the conversation he had with other soldiers, he made out that the number of persons killed at Pilica farm was inferior to the number of persons killed some days ago on 11 to 12 July in Kravica near Bratunac. This number was approximately 1300 killed Muslims." And then you go on and say: "According to Kos's words, special police units from Sehovici and Janja were supposed to take part in the killings as well." So you told the Slovenian investigator in 2004 that there were 1300, approximately 1300 killed Muslims at Kravica and the special police from Sehovici and Janja were involved; correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was already widely known and that's how the trial in The Hague was conducted, and I knew it from speaking to the -- to -- from hearing conversations between these people. But I didn't see the -- any people killed elsewhere, so I couldn't say if there were more or less. I only can speak about Branjevo and Kravica. These are things that I saw myself. And how many there were at Kravica in the warehouse, I cannot give you an exact number. It's only my estimate based on the size of the warehouse, and I think -- I made an estimate of how many people the warehouse could hold but it's merely my estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Right. So we can agree, your estimate isn't based on the number of bodies that you saw; it's based on what you remember from 18 years ago about the size of the warehouse; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, because as you can see in the picture, as far as I remember I told Investigator Blaszczyk that the left warehouse when I entered wasn't full, but that in the front part on the right it was empty, that there were no bodies or prisoners. That's about the left warehouse, whereas the right one was full.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Just one more thing on Kravica and then we'll move on. The DNA evidence in this case, again this is Mr. Janc's report, P4772, is the 1.374 individuals have been identified in the graves associated with the Kravica warehouse. Now, not all of those bodies come from the Kravica execution. There's around 1- to 200, we estimate, that come from other places. But that leaves 11- to 1200 individuals who are associated with the Kravica killings. Now, that's almost exactly the same number that you told the Slovenian investigator almost ten years ago in 2004, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only confirmed what people were saying about Kravica, and I must say that in that warehouse I said how many people there were. If there was another warehouse elsewhere, if -- whether there were people killed elsewhere, I can't say because I never saw that. And the DNA analyses performed have to do with the Kravica warehouse. But anyway, I only saw the warehouse at Kravica. I was in front and I went inside.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Now, Mr. President, I think my time's up. There are two short issues I'd like to deal with. It should be I think no more than 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: There was some questions the Chamber wondered whether you really had to put those questions, but what are the areas?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, one is related to the Pilica Dom and Mr. Kos's trip there after the Branjevo Farm which isn't dealt with at all in the Defence interview; and the second is very briefly the issuance of the false identification papers in 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Given the scheduling of today, we'll allow you to continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Kos, once your unit had finished at Branjevo Farm, you went to Pilica and sat in the cafe across the street from the Dom; correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And you went over to the Dom at one point and you looked inside, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I looked inside but I didn't enter, but I only approached the door to a distance of about 5 metres because there was some seven or eight bodies in front of the Dom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Well, when you looked inside you saw a lot of dead bodies, some wounded people inside the Dom; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there were bodies inside the Dom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And outside the Dom you could see there was some VRS military police, some civilian police, and some other soldiers standing around; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The military police was present all day and the civilian police, I don't know what they were doing there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And then after you'd gone and looked in the Dom, you came back to the cafe and Colonel Beara stood up and gave a speech, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that the colonel gave a speech before I went to the Dom. I mean, if you can call that a speech, because he was drunk and he was boasting.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Right. Well --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Transcript.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Very drunk."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Kos, you've testified in your own trial about this speech and you've also talked about it in your interview with the state court prosecutor, and you talked about it to Mr. Blaszczyk as well. And isn't it correct that Colonel Beara said the following words: "Soldiers, you have done a great job and the state will be grateful to you." That was what Colonel Beara said, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, all the soldiers present heard it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. And when you heard Colonel Beara say those words, you told Mr. Blaszczyk that that meant you knew that they were planning this all along; right? So when you heard Colonel Beara's words, that was the moment when you knew that these killings had all been planned; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my opinion; it wasn't the opinion of all the soldiers. I understood then that somebody had planned something, but who and what I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I only know that I had to do what we had done, but pursuant to whose orders? Most probably Colonel Brano Gojkovic, once he's arrested, will say because he talked to him personally.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Four or five days later, so after Branjevo Farm, after the Pilica Dom, you saw Lieutenant Pelemis in Bijeljina and you asked him what had happened, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I asked him when he came from Belgrade what had happened and that's because I had asked him earlier not to send us to such places, and he merely replied: Force majeure, don't ask me anything else. And that's what I did, or rather didn't do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And you understood that comment, force majeure, to mean that these killings were something that you shouldn't have done but the orders came from on high and it was something that you had to do; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we had to do it. And as for force majeure, when he said those words to me I understood -- our direct superior was Petar Salapura, he was the one who always issued us orders. I thought at the time that that Petar Salapura was that force majeure. I never saw him at such places. That was my opinion. That's how I had understood his words. That's why I never asked any more questions. I didn't have the top echelons in mind, such as the government or the Main Staff and so on. I thought that this force majeure was actually Petar Salapura.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Right. Now, after Colonel Beara's speech where he said that the state would be grateful to you, your unit wasn't investigated or prosecuted by the VRS, the RS MUP, the RS civilian authorities, or any other RS authorities, were they?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've just told you that I was told never to ask any questions about that again.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I'm asking you, you weren't investigated or prosecuted by any organ of the RS state, were you, so not the VRS, not the MUP, and not the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's true. Nobody ever asked me anything about the incident that happened at Branjevo Farm, that is, not before 2004.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. Can I have Exhibit P4491 in e-court.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: This is an order -- what you're about to see, Mr. Kos, is an order dated 16 January 1996 and it's from Dragan Kijac who was the minister of interior at the time to the head of the public security administration. And you can see Minister Kijac has cut and pasted the text of an order from -- or a request from Colonel Salapura which you can read there. It says: "Considering we have a group of members in the 10th Sabotage Detachment who are foreign citizens or who are on a list of individuals who have been indicted by the Hague Tribunal, we ask that you order the Bijeljina MUP to issue personal IDs with Serbian first and last names to these individuals or with different first and last names for Serbian nationals. There are eight such individuals." And over on the -- if we go to the next page we can see Minister Kijac passes this on and says to the public security administration: "You are required to act on the request ..." So eight false identifications for eight members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment. You received false identifications at around this time in the name of Branimir Manojlovic; correct?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And that's a Serbian first name and a Serbian last name; right?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. At the time you received your false --

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment. The family name is Serbian, but the first name is actually the name I was given at christening. My name is Branko, and that family name is my partner's name. However, on that ID, that was issued on the 8th of February, 1996. I entered my original identification number which I was issued with in Slovenia. Somebody didn't like that, so after a year I was given a different ID with a Bosnian ID number. As for this ID card, I cancelled that through the regular procedure at the Bijeljina SUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. At the time you received your false identification papers in February 2006, were you aware that the minister of interior had personally arranged for these false identification papers to be issued to you?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, we didn't know that the minister had organised that. We arrived at the barracks where we were billeted in Bijeljina and - how shall I put it? - the desk clerk told us that we had to fill out forms for IDs pursuant to an order issued by Colonel Salapura.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Okay. So let's just summarise. You weren't investigated by any RS state organs, you weren't prosecuted by any RS state organs, and the minister of interior, the most senior law enforcement official in the RS, personally arranged for fake IDs for eight members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment. Now all of that, what I've just described, is consistent with Colonel Beara's statement on the 16th of July, that the state would be grateful to you for what you did at Branjevo Farm, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before you answer, just a second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, if I could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: He raised an objection.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: If I could ask for the witness to take off his headphones --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: -- during this objection.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Kos, could you kindly take off your headphones.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: And perhaps Mr. Karadzic could make the objection in English.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Yes, I'll do. It seems to me that it is rather for the closing argument than to summarise and to repeat and to repeat and to repeat. I -- this is not a jury court and those effects are moot and senseless.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In particular the -- whether it was arranged by the minister personally was not confirmed by the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, the reason I put that "personally," Mr. President, is because Colonel Salapura's request goes to the minister personally. So the foundation for my question is the document itself, not the witness's confirmation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: While I tend to see a point of Mr. Karadzic's objection, but there's no basis to stop you from asking that question. But how much more do you need to conclude your cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: That's it, Mr. President. That's the last question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Very well. Yes, Mr. Kos. Do you remember the question, Mr. Kos?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're asking me if I knew or whether this document is accurate or what Beara said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: No --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- whether that was accurate, is that it?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then I will ask Mr. Mitchell to repeat his last question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. Kos, my last question was: You weren't investigated by the RS state authorities, you weren't prosecuted by the RS state authorities, and the minister of interior personally arranged for eight members of the 10th Sabotage Detachment, including you, to receive false identification papers. And all of that, what I've just described, is consistent with what Colonel Beara said in the cafe in Pilica on 16 July, that the state would be grateful to you, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: What you are just asking me I can answer only in this way: Judging by the document that I've been shown here, I can only conclude that the colonel of the intelligence centre, Petar Salapura, is hereby requesting the minister of the interior to issue IDs. This is Colonel Salapura's request. Minister Kijac approved the issuing of IDs as far as I know. This is not his request. This is Colonel Salapura's request.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: I'll leave it there, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. We'll have a break.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: I have only ten minutes, but if you think that the break is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It depends upon the tape and -- yeah, we have to have a break. We'll resume at ten past 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. I'd like to introduce to you and the Chamber Evangelia Miromidou, who is an intern working with us. She's from Greece and Bulgaria. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, Mr. Karadzic, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Kos, let us please clarify certain matters that were mentioned in cross-examination. Yesterday on page 90 of the transcript you said that you saw that there were cases when persons were being singled out. Some Serbs were looking for some particular Muslims and they expressed their rage. Did they take any Muslim or were they looking for a specific person whom they knew?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is a question for two different things. I saw with my own eyes that they knew each other in front of the warehouse in Kravica, so they were looking for them by name, such and such a person. As for taking things out on them, that was at the Branjevo Farm. They took them out one after the other and mistreated them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. That's also what you said to the Slovenian investigator on page 3, that is, 65 ter 25487. It says here: "The greatest atrocities were committed by the Serbs who had been expelled in the beginning of the war and who were forced to leave Srebrenica, to flee from Srebrenica." Do you stand by that today as well?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I stand by that now and I will always stand by that, that certain local persons, I'm not saying all of them, certain persons who had been mistreated by Muslims in the beginning of the war and who had lost some of their nearest and dearest took revenge against those people.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 2 today you said that - when speaking about the difference between the killed and the buried - you said that they were brought in the next day. Do you mean they were brought in on the next day and then killed or did you mean that bodies were brought in the next day?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next day. As far as I know through my own trial, they were brought on trucks, two trucks - bodies were brought on two trucks, that's what a witness said - that had been loaded at the Pilica Dom. So they were brought there dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you hear that a guard told Erdemovic before the executions that there had been burials there earlier, that he stated that during his testimony?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for that statement of Erdemovic's, I cannot confirm that because I saw that guard only on one occasion. When we came to the Branjevo Farm, he went to one of the rooms where -- well, I don't know. I think it says "uprava," the administration, on the sketch. And it was sort of like a stable -- no, a pigsty. I did not see that guard and I did not hear that conversation between them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. On page 5 you started to say the driver who brought from Bratunac and then you were interrupted. Do you remember now what it was that you wanted to say? So could you please finish that now?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can remember what I wanted to say. The bus driver who came from Bratunac, this is what he said, and now all of this adds on to the five buses, three buses, the question that was put here, the 16th but it happened on the 15th, and the bus driver made a statement before a court of law that they came from Bratunac with 12 buses and two trucks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I would object. If Mr. Kos is simply repeating evidence that he heard in his own trial rather than something that he saw or heard at the time, I don't think that has any probative value.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I'm sorry, repeating evidence that he heard?

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: He's repeating evidence that he heard in the state court during his own trial; he's not speaking from his own knowledge of what he heard or saw at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, the Prosecution is fond of asking the witnesses about how they learned after the events about what had happened in Srebrenica, including at trials or in coffee shops and other places. So he's not limited to giving his evidence about what he heard at the time. But the weight that the Chamber will give to that evidence can relate to what the source of it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, Mr. President, I --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Let's leave it. But relaying what he heard during his trial is of no point. Shall we continue, Mr. Karadzic?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right. But I would like to hear that. Actually, maybe we'll call the driver and he can tell us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can explain it in a different way. Five buses, three buses, that was said here. For five buses and three buses, it was said the 15th of July, and the Prosecution here persistently said that they brought prisoners to the Branjevo Farm in five buses which is not correct. All of this story about five buses, three buses, has to do with the 15th of July, because they were brought to the school and from the school in the evening, because there wasn't enough room, two or three buses were taken to the Dom. So that's it. Let us clarify this, five buses, three buses.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: If the Chamber would allow me to ask whether there were 12 buses and several trucks all together from Bratunac to the region.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us what did this bus driver say? Were they all transferred from Bratunac on 12 buses and a few trucks? Was it only for Branjevo? Or did this pertain to all of these locations?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second. Yes, Mr. Mitchell.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Mr. President, I think he needs to rephrase the question. He -- you just ruled that what the bus driver said in his trial isn't relevant. He can ask him if he knows, if Mr. Kos knows, how many buses and trucks came, but he shouldn't be leading a number and he shouldn't be asking him to repeat what the bus driver said in his own trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, I agree. Yes, Mr. Karadzic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Mr. Kos, did you know or did you find out in how many vehicles were all the prisoners transported from Bratunac to that zone?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I found out during the trial from a witness: Twelve buses, two trucks stopped at the Vidikovac hotel, stopped at Rocevic, and further on the school in Pilica called Kula, and then from Kula to the Pilica Dom. That is the story about these 12 buses and two trucks, what I know from the testimony, that they were brought to that zone. I don't know about the rest. I cannot give any comment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Kos, before the 16th of July, 1995, did you ever receive such a task or similar one, you as the -- as an individual or as a unit, did you ever receive orders to do something unlawful?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: By who, the commander? The superior?

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Anyone. Did anyone order you as an individual or as a unit to do something like that?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: Something against civilians? Well, it's not that civilians had to be liquidated ever, it was that civilians should be protected. That was the order always by the commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You were in Kravica and at Branjevo Farm. Did you find out the reason why these persons were killed at both locations?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not find out why they were killed. I can just say what was conveyed to me then at the Branjevo Farm, that they were war criminals.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Before the event in Kravica, before the incident with the grabbing of the weapon, did you ever find out about a plan to have people killed in Kravica?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard of any such plan and I did not know that people in Kravica had been killed until I came to Kravica and found out that there had been an incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you hear and see for yourself that anyone from your detachment, your unit, or from among the people who communicated with you had the intention of destroying the Bosnian Muslims as a religious group as a whole or in part?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: He can't possibly answer that question, Mr. President, speaking about other people's intentions and what's in other people's minds.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: But he can answer whether anyone gave any indication as to whether that was the reason.

utterances.speaker: MR. MITCHELL
utterances.text: Well, that wasn't the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Perhaps he can rephrase it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: I asked whether he had heard or seen, whether he had seen for himself that there had been such intentions?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Such intentions, I did not hear that they existed. I can only speak about certain comments, hatred between individuals, and - how do I put this? - this neighbour of mine killed my brother and I'm going to kill him. I did hear that. If I catch him, he's dead. That's how it was on one side and on the other side. As for masses, I never heard of anything like that and I did not hear of any such indications.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kos. My last question: Did you hear anyone claim that they were acting on my orders and instructions?

utterances.speaker: FRANC KOS [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never heard that anyone mentioned your name in terms of you having ordered something in respect of the 10th Sabotage Detachment.

utterances.speaker: MR. KARADZIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kos.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Excellencies, I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Well, that concludes your evidence, Mr. Kos. On behalf of the Chamber, I would like to thank you for your coming to The Hague to give it. You are free to go. Now I also thank Mr. Zecevic for his assistance. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: I wonder whether there's anything to raise before the recess?

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. President, I just had one thing I wanted to raise with you and that is relating to the monograph that was discussed yesterday with General Savcic which is Exhibit D42, marked as not admitted. And I just wanted to tell the Chamber that we are taking the allegations made by the Prosecution very seriously, and we're looking into exactly how that document was altered and we are going to make a report to the Chamber about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber would appreciate it. There's nothing to say about the pending motions, in particular, suspension and the severance motion. The Chamber will issue -- try to issue its decision as soon as it receives the Appeals Chamber's ruling on the clarification motion.

utterances.speaker: MR. ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. We also thought it would be best to wait for that, so we appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Tieger.

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I'm not sure that we addressed that issue specifically in our expedited response, but it's not entirely clear to me that the motion -- the latter motion filed by the Defence implicates in the same manner it may have previously the pending motion for clarification. It seemed to me it was much more concerned with the Trial Chamber's decision about what should be led in the interim, and therefore in a sense may have sort of set aside the temporary significance of the clarification decision that will follow. So that -- at least without putting further thought to it, we began to accelerate and expedite our response as soon as we saw it because we considered that, in fact, it seemed to be a position taken by the Defence irrespective of the timing of the clarification decision. But I -- I don't know the extent to which that -- I don't recall the extent to which that may have been alluded to in our response, and I just note that for the Court by way of consideration as it looks at the pleadings before it right now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Chamber is hopeful that it could issue the decision by the end of this week, but I'll leave it at that. Any other issues?

utterances.speaker: MR. TIEGER
utterances.text: I don't believe so, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Then I wish all the parties a restful recess. The hearing is adjourned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Tuesday, the 27th day of August, 2013, at 9.00 a.m. 21 22 23 24 25

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 11.33 a.m.,
